headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: Coherent, AppLovin, Expedia, Qualcomm and more
headlines.summary: These are the stocks posting the largest moves after hours.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: COHR, APP, EXPE & more Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves after the bell: Qualcomm — The chipmaker fell almost 6% despite reporting a slight earnings beat in its fiscal fourth-quarter financial report . Further, Qualcomm sees adjusted earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 per share in the current quarter, while analysts sought $2.26 per share, per FactSet. AppLovin — The AI stock surged more than 20% after the software company known for mobile game advertising posted third-quarter results that topped estimates. AppLovin posted adjusted EBITDA of $1.84 billion, greater than the $1.73 billion consensus estimate, according to FactSet. Revenue of $2.18 billion exceeded the forecast $2.07 billion. Expedia — Shares tumbled more than 7% after it delivered mostly weaker-than-expected guidance for the current quarter. The online booking company forecasts revenue between $3.69 billion and $3.75 billion in the fourth quarter, but analysts polled by FactSet on average expected $3.74 billion. The company, however, beat estimates for both earnings and revenue in the third quarter. Coherent — The optical materials company gained 7% after reporting adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share, compared to analysts polled by FactSet's estimates for $1.99 per share. Revenue also came in above estimates, as did guidance for the current quarter. Zillow — Shares sank more than 16% after the company missed on key metrics in its third-quarter earnings report. Adjusted earnings came in at 55 cents per share, compared to analysts polled by LSEG's estimates for 59 cents. Revenue also was weaker than expected, at $724 million compared to expectations for $754 million. Klaviyo – The maker of the customer relationship management platform slid about 5% even as the company reported third-quarter results that beat estimates. Klaviyo posted adjusted earnings of 22 cents per share on revenue of $387.2 million. The FactSet consensus called for 17 cents per share and $380 million. Klaviyo also lifted its full-year revenue guidance. MercadoLibre – The e-commerce platform slid about 7% after third-quarter earnings missed expectations. MercadoLibre earned $8.83 per share, compared to the FactSet consensus estimate of $9.27 a share. Revenue of $10.75 billion beat the estimate for $10.69 billion, however. Arm Holdings — Shares dipped almost 2% despite the designer of central processing units delivering a strong earnings report. The UK-based company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, compared to analysts polled by LSEG's consensus estimates for 47 cents Cava — Shares fell more than 11% after it reported third-quarter 2026 financial results , missing Wall Street expectations. Earnings came in at 11 cents a share, versus the LSEG consensus estimate for 12 cents. Cava posted revenue of $356 million, while analysts expected the number to be $359 million. Wolfspeed – The semiconductor manufacturer dropped 5% after posting a wider-than-expected loss in the fiscal first quarter. Wolfspeed's adjusted loss of $2.03 per share came in worse than the FactSet consensus estimate for a $1.99 per share loss. Figma — The software stock dropped almost 7% even after the cloud-based design platform posted third-quarter results that blew away expectations. Figma posted adjusted earnings of 10 cents a share on revenue of $391 million, while the LSEG consensus called for 5 cents a share and $376 million. HubSpot – Shares fell more than 8% after the company's fourth-quarter earnings and revenue guidance came up short of expectations. HubSpot expects to earn between $3.85 and $3.87 per share on revenue of $945 million to $947 million. Analysts polled by FactSet were looking for $4.09 in earnings per share and $964.9 million in revenue. However, the company's third-quarter earnings and revenue beat expectations. e.l.f. Beauty – Shares of the cosmetics company gained more than 4%. Fiscal second quarter results surpassed estimates, with e.l.f. posting adjusted earnings of $1.21 per share and revenue of $521 million. Analysts polled by LSEG sought 60 cents per share and $470 million. Snap – Shares of the social media company tumbled 7%. Third-quarter revenue of $1.72 billion narrowly missed the LSEG consensus estimate of $1.73 billion. Global daily active users also fell short of expectations, coming in at 495 million versus the StreetAccount consensus of 499 million. Dutch Bros — The coffee chain sank 19% after it cut its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to at least $380 million from a previous range of $385 million to $390 million. Same-store sales in the third quarter also came in weaker than expected at 4.4%, versus the StreetAccount consensus estimate of 4.6%. Fastly – The edge cloud platform saw shares plummet 16%, even as earnings and revenue in the third quarter topped estimates, as did guidance for the current quarter. The company announced Scott Lovett, president of Go To Market, will be retiring in 2027. — CNBC's Sarah Min, Sean Conlon, Ananya Chetia and Deena Zaidi contributed reporting

The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. In this article CVS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:23 04:23 CVS Health CEO on splitting into two companies: ‘We’re doing it out of a position of strength’ Squawk on the Street CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS closed more than 12% lower on Wednesday. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy. "So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added. A person walks into a CVS pharmacy near George Washington University in Washington, U.S., August 15, 2024. Kaylee Greenlee Beal | Reuters CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. How the CVS split would work On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split. In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent. "This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday. One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers. But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure." Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration. The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies. PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies. The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount. "In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement. McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter. Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners. As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027. Shares of the company closed more than 6% higher Wednesday. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share. Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion. The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount. McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates. The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. "In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well." France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests.
